payload.canonical_key: factor graph based generative model aggregates outputs from multiple noisy heuristics to produce high quality probabilistic training labels aggregation process resolves conflicts b
payload.core_idea: A factor graph-based generative model aggregates outputs from multiple noisy heuristics to produce high-quality probabilistic training labels. This aggregation process resolves conflicts between heuristics and estimates the true label distribution without requiring ground truth for the unlabeled data.
payload.discussion: This aggregation technique is critical for transforming sparse, noisy signals into a dense, reliable training signal. It enables the use of simple, imperfect rules that would be unusable individually but become powerful when combined statistically. The resulting probabilistic labels allow downstream scene graph models to be trained effectively even when only a few dozen labeled examples per relationship are available.
payload.evidence: The abstract explicitly mentions that heuristic outputs are aggregated using a factor graph-based generative model. It further notes that with as few as 10 labeled examples, this model creates sufficient training data to train state-of-the-art scene graph models.
payload.idea_text: A factor graph-based generative model aggregates outputs from multiple noisy heuristics to produce high-quality probabilistic training labels. This aggregation process resolves conflicts between heuristics and estimates the true label distribution without requiring ground truth for the unlabeled data.
payload.mechanism: The mechanism utilizes a probabilistic graphical model where nodes represent the true latent labels and the observed heuristic outputs. Factors in the graph encode the reliability of each heuristic and the correlations between them. By performing inference on this graph, the model computes posterior probabilities for each relationship in the unlabeled set, effectively denoising the weak supervision signals.

work_version_records.abstract: Visual knowledge bases such as Visual Genome power numerous applications in computer vision, including visual question answering and captioning, but suffer from sparse, incomplete relationships. All scene graph models to date are limited to training on a small set of visual relationships that have thousands of training labels each. Hiring human annotators is expensive, and using textual knowledge base completion methods are incompatible with visual data. In this paper, we introduce a semi-supervised method that assigns probabilistic relationship labels to a large number of unlabeled images using few labeled examples. We analyze visual relationships to suggest two types of image-agnostic features that are used to generate noisy heuristics, whose outputs are aggregated using a factor graph-based generative model. With as few as 10 labeled examples per relationship, the generative model creates enough training data to train any existing state-of-the-art scene graph model. We demonstrate that our method outperforms all baseline approaches on scene graph prediction by 5.16 recall@100 for PREDCLS. In our limited label setting, we define a complexity metric for relationships that serves as an indicator (R^2 = 0.778) for conditions under which our method succeeds over transfer learning, the de-facto approach for training with limited labels.
